open-question.question: How does a run of the on-demand suite name the host it drives (Claude Code, Antigravity, or Codex), and what does a run that names none do? The suite today is bound to Antigravity by module constants: it reads no pytest option or environment variable and parametrizes no test. The two choices are asked together because they constrain each other: a mechanism such as one parametrized case per host already fixes the unnamed run as every host, so not every pairing of mechanism and unnamed-run behaviour is viable.

How does the suite find the installed plugin copy of Claude Code and of Codex, whose host definitions record no install path? Antigravity's copy sits at the fixed global path ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn, held as a suite constant. On the maintainer's machine Claude Code loads the plugin straight from this checkout's hosts/claude through the directory marketplace, with versioned copies also under ~/.claude/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/, and Codex copies it at install time to a versioned directory under ~/.codex/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/.

What must the prerequisite check require of the chosen host's installed plugin copy before any test runs? For Antigravity it requires the copy to be byte-identical, file for file, to the committed built tree hosts/antigravity/. On Claude Code the plugin can be loaded directly from this checkout's hosts/claude through the directory marketplace, where that comparison holds trivially, and on Codex the copy is a snapshot of hosts/codex/plugins/cairn/ taken at install time under the version it was installed at.
open-question.alternative: The existing third prerequisite becomes the rule for all three hosts. The copy the chosen host actually loads must match that host's plugin directory in the committed built tree file for file, a missing or extra file included: hosts/claude/ for Claude Code, hosts/antigravity/ for Antigravity, hosts/codex/plugins/cairn/ for Codex. A mismatch stops the run with the one prerequisite line before any test. When Claude Code loads straight from this checkout's hosts/claude, the comparison passes trivially and is still made. One rule for every host, generalized from the check that already exists. It is the only check here that catches a stale copy carrying the current version number, which is the state found on 2026-11-09: the Antigravity copy and the Claude Code cache's 1.9.0 copy both report 1.9.0 and both differ from the built trees (both still hold shared/get-current-milestone.md and lack shared/resolve-milestone.md). Any file the host adds or rewrites at install time fails it. Nobody has checked whether codex plugin add copies hosts/codex/plugins/cairn/ verbatim. On Claude Code the check tells nothing new when the loaded copy is the checkout itself, and it means something only if the located copy is the one the CLI really loads. That depends on how the sibling question on installed copy location settles.

On Antigravity and Codex the installed copy must be byte-identical to the host's built plugin directory, missing and extra files included. On Claude Code the check compares no file contents. It requires instead that the plugin source the CLI reports for cairn@cairn is this checkout's hosts/claude, loaded through the directory marketplace, and it stops the run on any other source, a cached or published copy included, even one byte-identical to the built tree. Every failure stops the run with the one prerequisite line before any test. On Claude Code the check becomes one that can fail for a real reason: a load from the ~/.claude/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/ copies (the 1.9.0 one is stale) or from the published marketplace. A file comparison that always passes is replaced. Claude Code never needs a reinstall after a core/ change, because the checkout is what loads. Running the suite on Claude Code needs this checkout's directory marketplace. A contributor who installed from the published cairn-claude repository is refused even when that copy is identical. Two different kinds of check now sit behind one prerequisite line, and the Claude Code one relies on reading the plugin source from claude's own report. Whether that report is the right source depends on the sibling question on installed copy location.

On every host the comparison is limited to the plugin's four runtime directories (agents/, shared/, skills/, tools/). Within those directories the installed copy must be byte-identical to the built plugin directory, missing and extra files included. Files outside them are not compared: the manifest directory, README and other top-level files, and any metadata the host adds at install time. A mismatch stops the run with the one prerequisite line before any test. It still catches every stale skill, procedure, agent, or tool that the tests actually exercise, including a same-version stale copy. It also tolerates whatever a host writes beside the plugin at install time or rewrites in its manifest, which on Codex has not been checked hands-on. It is weaker than the full-tree rule that exists today: a stale or wrong manifest passes unseen, even though the host reads the manifest to load the plugin. The four-directory set becomes one more rule the suite holds, and it must be kept in step with the build's [layout] mapping if a fifth runtime directory is ever added.

On every host the check compares only the version: the version recorded in the installed copy's manifest, or the version the host's own plugin listing reports, must equal VERSION. A mismatch stops the run with the one prerequisite line before any test. File contents are not compared. It is the cheapest check and the most robust one. It reads one value through each host's own manifest or listing, so it does not depend on which files a host copies or adds at install time, and it catches the Codex 1.7.6 copy at once. VERSION changes only at a release, and the suite runs on unreleased changes. A stale copy at the current version passes: on 2026-11-09 the Antigravity copy and the Claude Code cache's 1.9.0 copy both report 1.9.0 and both differ from the built trees. The suite would then certify old text as working, and it would lose the protection the current Antigravity check gives.

On every host the installed copy is compared byte for byte, file for file, with the host's built plugin directory, as in the full-tree rule. A mismatch prints one line naming the first differing file, and the tests then run anyway against the installed copy. Only a missing CLI or a missing copy still stops the run. The suite can be run on purpose against a copy other than the built tree, such as a published release being checked after the fact or a hand-patched copy under investigation. The run still says plainly that the copy differs. It breaks the suite's convention that a prerequisite stops the run before any test and is never a skip. A pass against a stale copy then means as much as a pass against a fresh one to anything that reads only the outcome, including the release pre-flight's check g, which runs the suite and reads its result.

No host's installed copy is compared against anything. The prerequisite check keeps only that the host's CLI resolves on PATH and that an installed copy is present, and it drops the existing Antigravity byte comparison. Tests run against whatever copy is installed. It needs no per-host comparison logic and no knowledge of what each host's install leaves on disk. It never blocks a run over a difference in a file the tests do not touch. The suite exists to check the committed integration before it is committed or released. Without a freshness check it can pass on a copy that does not contain the change under test, or fail for reasons already fixed, and nothing reports which happened. It also removes a guard that already works for Antigravity.

open-question.question: Which of the assertions that read the host's own tool-call records do the tests keep on all three hosts? Today the plugin-root test reads Antigravity's stream-json records to assert that no agent was dispatched, that a file read under the installed root's shared/ directory completed, and that a shell call running task_list.py insert under that root completed; each dispatch test reads them to assert exactly one dispatch of the named agent with the given prompt and no write or shell tool used by the dispatching process. Claude Code (--output-format stream-json) and Codex (codex exec --json) emit records of other shapes that the repository holds no parser for, and every other assertion of the three tests reads only files and git state.

What becomes of the plugin-root test's assertion that every file read attempted with a ~ path ended in ERROR, given that every test of the host-generic suite is to check behaviour that is the same on every host? The assertion pins that Antigravity's file-reading tool refuses the tilde literal its tree renders as the plugin root; the Claude Code and Codex trees render the root as a variable the host resolves, so no tilde path arises there.

How do the two agent-dispatch tests get their agent dispatched on each host? Today each test's own prompt tells the headless process to call Antigravity's invoke_subagent with the agent's bare name and the real three-line dispatch prompt, so no orchestrator skill stands between the test and the agent. Claude Code dispatches through its Agent tool by the namespaced name cairn:<agent>, and Codex registers no agent name: its orchestrators start a generic subagent whose prompt opens by telling it to read the plugin's agent file under the installed root.

What bounds a headless run of the suite on Claude Code and on Codex? The suite holds no wall-clock limit of its own: each Antigravity run is bounded only by agy's own --print-timeout 20m, and neither claude nor codex exec lists a time limit for a print run in its help.
open-question.alternative: The suite gains one wall-clock limit of its own, enforced the same way for all three hosts: the shared run fixture passes a timeout to the subprocess it starts (20 minutes, the value agy's run carries today, one value for every host), and a run that exceeds it is killed and fails its test. agy's --print-timeout is dropped from its command line, so the suite's limit is the only bound on every host. One bound, one value, and one expiry behaviour on all three hosts, owned and tested by the suite itself rather than by three CLIs, which fits the goal that only the prerequisite check and the invocation differ per host. Expiry becomes a killed process rather than a host's own orderly stop, so the test sees a Python timeout with no closing result record, and killing only the direct child can leave the host's own child processes (dispatched agents, shells) running unless the runner starts the process in its own session and kills its whole group; agy loses the native timeout its run relies on today.

The suite gains the same one wall-clock limit on every host, enforced through the subprocess timeout and killing the run on expiry, while agy keeps --print-timeout 20m on its command line as well; the suite's limit is set somewhat above agy's so that agy's own timeout fires first on Antigravity and the suite's limit is the only bound on Claude Code and Codex. Every host is bounded by a limit the suite owns, and Antigravity keeps its orderly native stop and its existing run unchanged, the suite's kill catching only a run that hangs past agy's own timeout. Two bounds with two values to keep in step on Antigravity, and the hosts still differ in how a run ends (a native stop on Antigravity, a kill elsewhere), with the same process-group cleanup needed for the kill.

Each host is bounded by its own native time limit where its CLI has one and by a suite wall-clock limit where it has none: agy keeps --print-timeout 20m as its only bound, and the claude and codex runs get a subprocess timeout of the same 20 minutes, killing the run on expiry. No spend or turn cap is added. Leaves the Antigravity run exactly as it is and adds a bound only where one is missing, the smallest change that gives every host a limit. The bound is a per-host branch in the runner, native on one host and suite-side on two, so the three hosts end a stuck run differently, and the moment a host's CLI gains or loses a native timeout the branch has to follow it.

As in the native-bound option, agy keeps --print-timeout 20m and the claude and codex runs get a suite subprocess timeout, but each host's limit is its own value rather than one shared 20 minutes, set from how long that host's runs of the three tests are observed to take (a longer one where its agent dispatch runs slower). Each limit can sit close to its host's real run time, so a hung run is cut off sooner on a fast host while a slower host is not killed mid-run by a limit sized for another. Three values to choose and keep current from observation, none of which the repository records today since no automated test has driven claude or codex, and a per-host value needs a per-host home, which depends on where the suite's per-host values live.

As in the native-bound option, agy keeps --print-timeout 20m and the claude and codex runs get a 20-minute suite subprocess timeout, and the claude run also passes --max-budget-usd with a fixed cap, the one run limit claude's help lists; codex, whose exec help lists neither a time nor a spend limit, gets the wall-clock limit alone. A runaway Claude Code run is stopped by the host itself on cost, with its own orderly ending, as well as by the wall clock, guarding against the expensive failure the suite's real-account runs at the default model can produce. Adds a dollar figure to choose and keep current that bounds cost, not time, applies to one host only, and can stop a legitimate run whose spend varies with the account's model, so a budget stop is a new failure mode the tests have to tell apart from a real defect.

Each test of the suite is bounded at the test level by a per-test timeout plugin (pytest-timeout added as a development dependency, one limit applied to every test on every host), rather than at the process level; agy's --print-timeout is kept or dropped as the native option keeps it, and no subprocess timeout is passed. One declared limit covers the whole test, the run and its assertions alike, on every host, with no timeout code in the run fixture. Adds a third-party dependency to a repository whose tools are stdlib-only and whose suites carry none, and the plugin's signal or thread method interrupts the test without reliably killing the host process it started, so a hung CLI can outlive its failed test.

The suite adds no limit for Claude Code or Codex: the claude and codex runs carry no timeout, no spend cap, and no turn cap and run until the CLI exits, while agy keeps its native --print-timeout 20m; a stuck run is ended by the maintainer interrupting the suite, which is on-demand and run by hand. No new code, value, or dependency, and nothing that can kill a legitimate slow run, for a suite that is never unattended: it sits outside testpaths and CI and is run by the maintainer before committing or releasing. A hung Claude Code or Codex run blocks the session indefinitely with no failure reported, which also stalls the release pre-flight's run of the suite, and the hosts differ in whether a run can hang at all.

open-question.question: Under which approval and sandbox mode does the suite run codex exec? docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md documents the headless form with --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox, while the Codex host definition's hands-on check was made under the workspace-write sandbox. The tests have the run commit in a git repository seeded under pytest's temporary directory and have the dispatched agents write to a scratch directory created there too.
open-question.alternative: Every Codex run of the suite passes --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox, the flag docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md gives for headless Codex chains: no approval prompts and no sandbox, so the seeded repository under tmp_path, its .git directory, and the test-created scratch directory are all writable with no further flag. The mode is fixed in the suite, not chosen per run. The suite drives Codex exactly as the documented headless chains do and on the same footing as the --dangerously-skip-permissions it already passes to agy (and would pass to claude), so a pass says the chains users actually run work, and no sandbox write rule can fail a test for a reason unrelated to the plugin. It never exercises the workspace-write sandbox that the Codex hands-on check of 2026-10-13 was made under and that the alternatives-agent contract relies on when it says the mktemp -d scratch directory stays writable under that sandbox, so a regression there goes unseen; and each run executes model-generated commands unsandboxed under the user's real HOME.

Every Codex run passes -s workspace-write with approvals turned off (-c approval_policy="never" or the equivalent), and nothing else: no --add-dir and no writable-root override, so the scratch directory is writable only through workspace-write's default writable temp locations and the seeded repository as the run's working root. The mode is fixed in the suite. It runs under the same sandbox as the recorded hands-on check and tests, rather than assumes, the claim the alternatives-agent return contract makes: that a scratch directory under the system temp location is writable under workspace-write's defaults, as the orchestrators' real runs leave it. It diverges from the documented headless form, so a pass does not vouch for the chains docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md shows; the commit-making tests depend on the sandbox letting git write the seeded repository's .git directory, and the scratch test on pytest's tmp_path lying under the temp location the sandbox treats as writable, neither of which the repository records as checked, so a test can fail for a sandbox rule rather than the plugin (whether such a failure is fixed in the plugin is the host-integration-defects question's to settle).

Every Codex run passes -s workspace-write with approvals turned off, plus --add-dir naming the test's tmp_path (or the scratch directory and the seeded repository explicitly), so every directory a test writes is a declared writable root whatever the sandbox's temp defaults are. The mode is fixed in the suite. It keeps the run sandboxed, matching the hands-on check's mode, while making the tests' writes independent of where pytest puts tmp_path and of which temp locations the sandbox writes by default, so a sandbox-default change on a Codex upgrade does not fail the suite. It tests a configuration no real orchestrator run uses, since neither the documented chains nor the skills pass --add-dir, so it masks exactly the default-writability the scratch-directory contract claims; it still differs from the documented bypass form; and declared writable roots may still leave .git protected, the same unverified commit risk as plain workspace-write.

Every Codex run passes --approve-for-me, keeping the workspace-write sandbox but routing every approval request, a write outside the writable roots or into .git included, through Codex's automatic review instead of failing it. No --add-dir; the mode is fixed in the suite. A test keeps the sandbox the hands-on check used, yet an escalation the sandbox would otherwise refuse in a non-interactive run can still be granted, so a commit or a scratch write is less likely to fail the test for a sandbox rule alone. Each escalation is decided by a reviewing model, so whether a test passes can vary run to run for reasons outside the plugin, and the runs get slower; the mode is documented nowhere in the repository and matches neither the documented headless form nor the hands-on check's setup.

Codex runs of the suite exercise two modes: each Codex test runs once under the documented --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox and once under -s workspace-write with approvals off and no added roots, as two parametrized cases or two selectable values of the run's Codex invocation. A pass covers both the chains docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md documents and the sandbox the hands-on check and the scratch-directory contract rely on, so neither form can regress unseen. It doubles the slowest runs in the suite (each a full headless model session) on Codex alone, and how the second mode is selected depends on the host-selection-per-run question's mechanism; it also carries the workspace-write mode's unverified .git and tmp_path writability risk into every run.

The suite passes no sandbox or approval flag to codex exec and runs under whatever the user's ~/.codex/config.toml and Codex's exec defaults give. The suite carries no Codex-specific mode at all, and a run checks the plugin under the configuration the maintainer actually uses day to day. The outcome is not reproducible across machines or Codex upgrades: a default that sandboxes writes or raises an approval request a non-interactive run cannot answer fails the writing and committing tests for a reason the suite neither states nor checks, and the prerequisite check has nothing to verify.

open-question.question: What is the host-generic suite called? The name is carried by its directory at the repository root (today agy_tests/), by its command (uv run pytest agy_tests), by the prose that refers to it (the agy suite), and by the one line its prerequisite check prints (agy suite prerequisite missing: ...), which the release pre-flight quotes.

Is the suite's fixture project, tracked at tests/fixtures/agy_project/, renamed along with the suite? Its path is named in CLAUDE.md's milestones-tool invariant and in the suite's conftest, and tests/test_milestones_tasks.py uses it as a synthetic commit path in three tests.
open-question.alternative: The fixture project stays at tests/fixtures/agy_project/ under its current name and location. conftest's FIXTURE_PROJECT path and the milestones.fixture/ container stay unchanged, and so do the four tests/fixtures/agy_project/… synthetic commit paths in tests/test_milestones_tasks.py. In CLAUDE.md the path in the milestones-tool invariant and in the layout entry stays as it is, and only the surrounding words naming the suite change with the suite's rename. Nothing outside the suite's own references changes. The tracked path keeps matching the history that created it, including 2202e59, which the tasks join keeps under its placeholder and which a comment in test_milestones_tasks.py cites. The tests of an unrelated tool are not touched. A host-generic suite would be seeded from a directory named after a single host. The goal says the suite's name and every reference to it should follow the rename, and this leaves a misleading agy reference in CLAUDE.md's invariant, its layout entry, and the conftest.

The fixture project is renamed under tests/fixtures/ to a name built from the suite's new name, with the agy_ prefix replaced. It keeps its milestones.fixture/ container. conftest's FIXTURE_PROJECT and seeded_repo docstring, CLAUDE.md's milestones-tool invariant and layout entry, and the four synthetic commit paths in tests/test_milestones_tasks.py all change to the new path in the same change. The fixture's name, the suite's name, and every path that mentions them stay aligned. A reader of CLAUDE.md or the milestones tool's tests sees a real current path, not one that only exists in history. The fixture's name depends on the suite's name, which the Suite directory name question decides, and a later suite rename would mean renaming the fixture again. The change also edits the tests of an unrelated tool, test_milestones_tasks.py, for a path those tests never read.

The fixture project is renamed under tests/fixtures/ to a host-neutral name that describes what it holds, such as the seeded pocket-ledger project. The name is independent of whatever the suite is called. It keeps its milestones.fixture/ container. conftest, CLAUDE.md's milestones-tool invariant and layout entry, and the four synthetic commit paths in tests/test_milestones_tasks.py all change to the new path in the same change. The host-specific name goes away without tying the fixture to the suite's name. It reads correctly whatever the Suite directory name question decides, and no later suite rename forces a second fixture rename. The fixture's name and the suite's name stop matching, so the link between them is carried only by conftest's FIXTURE_PROJECT and CLAUDE.md's prose. It also has the same churn in test_milestones_tasks.py as any rename that updates those strings.

The fixture project is renamed under tests/fixtures/ to a host-neutral name, taken either from the suite's name or from its contents. conftest and CLAUDE.md's milestones-tool invariant and layout entry follow the new name. The four tests/fixtures/agy_project/… strings in tests/test_milestones_tasks.py are left as they stand, as synthetic paths that never read the fixture. Every live reference to the fixture loses the host name, while the change stays inside the suite and CLAUDE.md. The milestones tool's tests, which pass with any synthetic path, are left alone, and their strings keep matching the historical path that 2202e59, cited in a comment there, actually changed. Those three tests would name a nested-project path that no longer exists in the tree. Their realism, which models this repository's own fixture, quietly becomes historical, and a later reader may take the agy_project strings for a leftover the rename missed.

The fixture project moves out of tests/fixtures/ into the suite's own directory at the repository root, for example as a project/ subdirectory beside its conftest, keeping its milestones.fixture/ container. conftest's FIXTURE_PROJECT and CLAUDE.md's milestones-tool invariant and layout entry change to the new path, and so do the synthetic commit paths in tests/test_milestones_tasks.py. The on-demand suite becomes self-contained, and any rename of the suite carries its fixture with it, now and later. tests/fixtures/ is left holding only fixtures of the default pytest suite, which the on-demand fixture never served. It breaks the repository's convention that every fixture lives under tests/fixtures/, and it moves tracked files, so their history needs --follow. The final path also depends on the suite's directory name, which the Suite directory name question decides.

open-question.question: How do the installed plugin copies get brought up to date so that this milestone's tasks can run the suite to a pass on all three hosts? The suite writes nothing to the installation it drives and stops before any test when the copy differs from the built tree. On the maintainer's machine, checked 2026-11-09, the Antigravity copy differs from hosts/antigravity/ and Codex holds cairn 1.7.6, a tree older than hosts/codex/plugins/cairn/.

Against which hosts does the release pre-flight run the suite, and on which changed paths? Today check g runs the Antigravity-only suite when git diff since the last release tag prints anything under scripts/hosts/antigravity/, core/agents/*.md, scripts/build_hosts.py, or agy_tests/, and CONTRIBUTING.md asks for a run before committing a change to the same path set, which names neither the Claude Code nor the Codex host definition. The two choices are asked together because they constrain each other: running only the hosts a change touched needs trigger paths kept per host, which one shared path set cannot give.

Where do the suite's per-host values live: the CLI command and its flags, the plugin directory in the built tree, the installed root, and whatever tool names and record shapes the tests read? Today they are Antigravity-bound module constants and fixtures in the suite's Python files, while everything else about a host is declared under scripts/hosts/<host>/, where adding a host needs no host-specific Python.

Does this milestone update the dated hands-on blocks heading scripts/hosts/claude/settings.toml and scripts/hosts/codex/settings.toml once the suite passes on those hosts? Each block is the one record of a host's hands-on check, naming the installed version and the points the run covered. Antigravity's cites the suite for its 2026-10-26 re-check; Claude Code's (2026-10-18, claude 2.1.302, its dispatch points carried forward unchecked from 2026-10-13) and Codex's (2026-10-13, under the workspace-write sandbox) record manual runs only.

When a suite test fails on a host because of the plugin's integration for that host and not because of the suite, is fixing the plugin (a slot value, a host definition, or a file under core/) part of this milestone? The goal requires the three existing tests to pass against all three hosts, and no automated test has driven claude or codex before.
